citations.quote: This paper presents an innovative approach that combines the concurrent engineering paradigm with standardized calculation sheets linked to a CubeSat Technologies Database, facilitating the preliminary design process and enabling component selection based on applicable specifications and performance data of available technology.

This combined concurrent design approach offers faster, more flexible, and transparent design management compared to traditional methods, simplifying the system design flow and the decision-making process in the early phases of a space mission project.

This approach has been implemented and tested during several CubeSats projects, among them an in-orbit servicing cis-lunar mission and a CubeSat constellation around Bennu asteroid, emphasizing collaborative learning through concurrent design sessions, and encouraging both communication and resource sharing across different technical fields.

In contrast to traditional document-centric systems engineering methods, CE and MBSE rely on computer-based tools and procedures to improve the design, development, and verification process of space systems by enabling a structured and digitally processable expression of information through digital models and tools, which are used as the primary means of information exchange.

The fundamental principles of the Concurrent Model-Based approach are simultaneous system modelling and iterative design refinement: multiple teams work concurrently on various aspects of the system, using models and tools to represent their respective disciplines.

This allows teams to collaborate effectively by sharing and exchanging models, ensuring consistency and alignment across the system. Parallel system development and early identification of potential issues and risks ensures a continuous refinement of the models and leads to optimized system design.

Furthermore, by integrating the models early in the development process, the system compatibility can be assessed, reducing errors and minimising potential conflicts, and the verification process can begin in advance with respect to traditional methodologies.
The S3D Tool is intended to facilitate the design process, by performing the CubeSat subsystems sizing and evaluating the system budgets.

It consists of a set of calculation sheets implemented in Microsoft Excel dedicated to the main disciplines of the preliminary design phase of a CubeSat project: Attitude Determination and Control System (ADCS), Communication System (CommSys), Electrical Power System (EPS), Propulsion System, Thermal Control System (TCS), Optical Payload, Risk, and Cost.
Each spreadsheet is described in detail in a user manual, from the assumptions used to the mathematical formulas employed to a step-by-step guide to compiling the different sheets.
In addition, a central repository, called Central Data Exchange System, was created to facilitate communication and information management during the design process.

This repository is linked to the other spreadsheets and allows for both automated and manual data input. Its purpose is to ensure that up-to-date information and data are shared across different disciplines and levels (mission, system, subsystem, component) while verifying that all disciplines operate on the same assumptions.
Indeed, an alert system consisting of a Check column for the input values in common between two or more disciplines has been implemented in the central repository.

The ADCS, CommSys, EPS, Propulsion, Thermal, and Payload sheets are linked to the corresponding spreadsheet, allowing an automatic filling of the 'Inputs' and 'Outputs' tables and ensuring a consistency check on the inputs.

The current version of the CUTE-DB is an Excel-based database, covering several CubeSat technologies such as Deployers, Structures, Command and Data Handling (C&DH) systems, EPS, ADCS, CommSys, Propulsion Systems, Navigation Systems, Optical Payloads, TCS, Docking Systems, Mechanisms, and Platforms.

The database structure is kept consistent throughout the different sheets, where the properties of each technology and their relationships are highlighted, representing a picture of what is currently available in the market.
The CUTE-DB has been populated using several sources available online [11, 12], as well as official developer websites, and it is currently updated to June 2024.

As per [13, 14], this process has been adapted, reducing the workflow into four, 4-hour sessions, structured as follows: (i) Session 1: Kick-off & Start of mission design - the mission objectives, study requirements and drivers are presented. A preliminary mission analysis is performed, and different Concepts of Operations (ConOps) and mission architectures are identified. In addition, a preliminary cost and risk assessment is initiated; (ii) Session 2: Mission design ConOps and mission architecture are consolidated, while the mission analysis is iterated, defining the Delta-V. The system architecture is defined, and the preliminary subsystem architectures are outlined. Cost and risk assessments are further elaborated; (iii) Session 3: System design - system and subsystem budgets are computed, and preliminary subsystems sizing is carried out; (iv) Session 4: Consolidation of baseline - finalization of the iteration(s), up to the selection of the subsystem-level components.

Each session starts with a 15-minute kick-off, in which an overview/summary of the project status is given to enable everyone to start with a clear idea of the assumptions to be used. In addition, the main objectives of the session are explained, and the main tasks are presented. The kick-off is followed by 3.5 hours of iteration work, during which the baseline study is performed, following the previously presented objectives and tasks, and the team continuously communicates, discusses, and takes decisions by consensus. Finally, the last 15 minutes of the session are dedicated to an internal presentation where each expert presents their work, the results are discussed and the next steps of the study are defined, to be carried out in the next concurrent session.

Although the Concurrent Model-Based approach can be applied to multiple teams, the concurrent design sessions have been managed by a single team of 12 members, each with a specific role and tasks to be accomplished during the sessions.

Therefore, the Concurrent Model-Based approach and the related tools (both S3D Tool and CUTE-DB) have been implemented and tested in several case studies, including the Bennu Observer Small Satellites (BOSS) mission, the Geo-Profundo mission [13], and the Cislunar mission [15].
The BOSS mission is a feasibility study of a CubeSat mission, with the aim to conduct in-situ observations of the Bennu asteroid, a near-Earth object (NEO).

The mission architecture is based on a motherdaughter configuration, in which the mothercraft provides the interplanetary transfer of the small satellite(s) to the asteroid, a safe deployment in the proximity of the asteroid, and relays communications to/from Earth.
By implementing the Concurrent Model-Based approach, four concurrent design sessions have been carried out.

During Session 3, the subsystems sizing and the preliminary selection of Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) components have been addressed, concurrently with mission analysis iterations. In addition, system budgets have been computed.

Finally, Session 4 allowed iterations to be concluded, the subsystem components selected, and the final system budgets computed, consolidating the baseline. The cost budget and the risk assessment, including the mitigation actions to be applied, have been finalized.

The methodology has also been applied to the feasibility study of the in-orbit servicing of multi-purpose autonomous CubeSat inspectors in proximity of the Lunar Gateway [15].

The results of the concurrent design sessions of the BOSS mission were presented in 3.2, and now the effectiveness of the Concurrent Model-Based approach is discussed, comparing the feasibility study results obtained from the concurrent design sessions with the same study conducted with the traditional methodology.

The CE-MBSE methodology resulted in a spacecraft mass of 22.59 kg, which is approximately 15% lower than the 26.6 kg calculated using the traditional methodology. This reduction in mass is likely due to the integrated, iterative nature of the concurrent approach, allowing design teams to identify and eliminate inefficiencies earlier in the process.

The CE-MBSE approach produced a Delta-V budget of 1.33 m/s, nearly double the 0.68 m/s calculated using the traditional methodology. This may be due to the time allocated for the feasibility analysis, which, using the traditional methodology, allowed for more iteration and refinement in the trajectory analysis.
However, the shown results only take into account the 4 sessions results and not the post-study refinement.

The CE-MBSE approach projected a total mission cost of 15 million euros, which is significantly lower than the 22 million euros estimated through the traditional approach. This cost efficiency likely stems from the concurrent design's ability to minimize redesigns, optimize resources, and reduce the need for extensive iterations across different teams.

Using the CE-MBSE methodology, the feasibility study was completed in one month, compared to the three months required when using the traditional approach. This shortened timeline reflects the enhanced collaboration and integration made possible by concurrent engineering, where multiple teams work in parallel rather than waiting for sequential handoffs.

Firstly, the S3D Tool needs to be improved and optimised. A preliminary calculation sheet for the Optical Payload has been developed to support initial design and performance evaluations. However, this sheet needs to be updated to reflect the latest design changes and integrated into the central repository to ensure alignment with the overall system design and easy access by all team members.

Beyond the Optical Payload, a similar calculation sheet dedicated to the Command & Data Handling (C&DH) subsystem must also be created to standardize performance calculations and requirements tracking across all key systems. This will improve the consistency and efficiency of the design process.

Additionally, alternative environments are currently under investigation to complement or replace the current tools in use. Specifically, software environments such as Comet and Matlab's System Composer are being explored for their potential to offer enhanced systems engineering capabilities, such as improved model-based design, architecture definition, and real-time collaboration features.

Furthermore, a discussion on CUTE-DB is open among the research team: to optimize the database management system used in the project, other environments are being evaluated, with MySQL being a key candidate under investigation [16].

By integrating the principles of Concurrent Engineering and Model-Based Systems Engineering, this methodology not only streamlines the design process but also enhances collaboration among diverse stakeholders, fostering a more efficient development environment.

The Concurrent Model-Based approach combines the principles of CE and MBSE to achieve a more efficient and effective system design process for micro and nanosatellite missions and services, offering several advantages over conventional methods, including faster design processes, enhanced flexibility, and improved transparency.
